summary: Libya requires a visa for nearly every nationality. The tourist visa is applied for online through Libya's eVisa portal and must be sponsored by a tourism company registered with the passports authority; other visa types cannot yet be applied for online. Only Algeria, Malaysia, Mauritania and Tunisia are listed as visa-exempt. The country remains divided and high-risk.

currencyLimits.text: Declare cash worth more than USD 10,000 to customs when you enter or leave Libya, or it may be confiscated and you may be detained. Taking Libyan dinar out of Libya is illegal.

notes: Alcohol is prohibited in Libya — do not bring any in, including duty-free.
Photography of checkpoints, military sites and infrastructure can lead to detention — always ask before photographing people.

payments.text: Libya runs on cash — international cards are effectively unusable and banks suffer chronic banknote shortages. Bring US dollars or euros in cash and exchange as needed through your host or operator.

safety.text: Libya remains divided between rival administrations with armed groups active across the country. The UK advises against all travel except to Tripoli, Misrata and the Benghazi–Jebel Akhdar area, and against all but essential travel to those, citing armed clashes, terrorism, kidnapping, detention and unexploded ordnance; in-person consular help is not available in Libya.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Libya travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: Spring and fall are mildest on the Mediterranean coast; the desert interior is best in the cooler months from October to April.

tips.text: Western governments uniformly advise against all travel to Libya — armed conflict can reignite with little warning, kidnapping and detention of foreigners occur, and most embassies operate from outside the country.

No sponsor, no visa: a tourist visa application on Libya's eVisa portal must be sponsored by a tourism company registered with the Passports, Nationality and Foreigners Affairs Authority, and must include the company's letter naming the tour group and destination. The small number of operators running escorted tours handle this for you.

Libya is split between rival governments in the west and east — approvals and paperwork valid for Tripoli-controlled territory may not be honored in the east and vice versa, so your itinerary must match the authority that approved your entry.
Bring all funds in cash (US dollars or euros). Cards do not work, ATMs cannot be relied on, and the dinar cannot be exchanged abroad.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Libya?
faq.answer: Yes, unless you hold an Algerian, Malaysian, Mauritanian or Tunisian passport — Libya's eVisa portal lists only those four as exempt. Everyone else needs a visa arranged before travel; tourists apply online through the eVisa portal, sponsored by a tourism company registered with the Passports, Nationality and Foreigners Affairs Authority.

faq.question: Is Libya open for tourism?
faq.answer: Only marginally. A handful of accredited operators run escorted tours to sites such as Leptis Magna, Sabratha and the old city of Tripoli, arranging the mandatory invitation and security. Independent tourism is not possible, and Western governments advise against all travel.

faq.question: Does Libya have an eVisa or visa on arrival?
faq.answer: Libya has an eVisa: tourist visas are applied for online at evisa.gov.ly, sponsored by a registered Libyan tourism company, and the visa is sent by email. It is the only visa type the portal accepts online so far. No official source describes a visa on arrival.

faq.question: Is it safe to visit Libya?
faq.answer: No — Libya is rated do-not-travel by Western governments. The country remains split between rival armed administrations, fighting can resume suddenly, and kidnapping and arbitrary detention of foreigners occur. Any visit requires professional arrangements through an accredited operator.

faq.question: Can I enter Libya with an Israeli passport or Israeli stamps?
faq.answer: No — Israeli passport holders are not admitted to Libya, and evidence of travel to Israel in any passport can also lead to refusal.
